title.en: Practice: Decision making: reading the situation and choosing a course of action
title.hi: अभ्यास: निर्णयन: स्थिति को पढ़ना और कार्रवाई चुनना

section: Practice (written by us, not from a UPSC paper): Decision making: reading the situation and choosing a course of action

en.stem: You head a district office. A villager complains in writing that a clerk in your office asked for money to process a certificate. There is no other evidence yet. What should you do first?
options: Suspend the clerk at once
Have the complaint verified promptly, hear the clerk, and see that the villager's certificate is processed without delay
Tell the villager that such things happen and to come another day
Transfer the clerk quietly to avoid trouble
en.why: The complaint is not yet a finding, so punishment now is out of proportion and unfair. Doing nothing leaves the villager without help. The second option deals with the villager's need and starts a fair check.

en.stem: You are a junior engineer. Your senior tells you orally to certify a stretch of road as complete although the last layer has not been laid. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Certify it, since the senior is responsible
Refuse and stop coming to the site
Complain to a newspaper
Explain to the senior that the work is incomplete, decline to sign a false certificate, and ask for the instruction in writing if it is repeated
en.why: A false certificate is unlawful whoever orders it. The fourth option states the concern, keeps within the role, and creates a record. Walking away or going to the press skips the proper steps.

en.stem: You are in charge of a relief camp after a flood. Drinking water will last only until evening and the next supply is due tomorrow noon. What should you do?
options: Arrange water at once from the nearest available source, ration what remains, and inform your seniors as you do so
Write to headquarters and wait for a reply
Tell the people in the camp to manage on their own
Wait for tomorrow's supply as scheduled
en.why: Harm is near, so action comes first and paperwork follows. The first option protects people now and keeps seniors informed.

en.stem: You are an officer deciding applications for a licence. A relative of yours has applied and asks you to clear the file quickly. What should you do?
options: Clear it first, since you know the applicant is honest
Reject it, to show that you are impartial
Disclose the relationship to your senior and ask that another officer decide the file in its turn
Keep the file pending indefinitely
en.why: This is a conflict of interest. Favouring the relative and punishing the relative are both unfair. Disclosure and stepping aside keep the decision on its merits.

en.stem: You manage a ration shop inspection team. An elderly woman's fingerprint does not match on the machine and the dealer refuses her grain. The rules allow another method of identification in such cases. What should you do?
options: Tell her to come again next month
Direct the dealer to use the alternative method the rules allow and give her the grain, and note the failure for correction
Buy grain for her with your own money
Cancel the dealer's licence on the spot
en.why: The rules already provide the answer, so the task is to apply them and record the fault. Paying from your pocket helps one person and leaves the fault in place. Cancelling the licence without a hearing is out of proportion.

en.stem: You are a team leader. Two members blame each other for a missed deadline, and the work is still not done. What do you do first?
options: Report both to the head of the organisation
Do the work yourself and say nothing
Decide who is at fault and warn that person in front of the team
Get the remaining work divided and finished, then find out with both what went wrong
en.why: The work is the immediate need; the cause can be examined fairly afterwards with both present. A public warning before the facts are clear is unfair, and passing it upward avoids your own job.

en.stem: You are a tax officer. A person whose case is before you sends a costly gift to your home on a festival. What should you do?
options: Return the gift, record the fact as the rules require, and decide the case on its merits
Keep it, since refusing would be rude
Keep it but decide the case strictly
Decide the case against the person to prove your honesty
en.why: Accepting a gift from a person with a pending case is improper whatever the later decision. Deciding against the person to prove a point is as unfair as favouring them.

en.stem: You are a school principal. Parents complain that a teacher often comes late. The teacher has a good record in other respects. What should you do?
options: Ignore the complaint because of the good record
Recommend the teacher's removal
Check the attendance record, speak to the teacher privately to learn the reason, and set a clear expectation
Announce the complaint in the staff meeting
en.why: Verify, hear, then act in proportion. A good record is a reason for a private conversation first, not a reason to ignore the matter.

en.stem: You are a municipal officer. A hospital asks you to waive a mandatory fire-safety inspection so that a new ward can open a week early. What should you do?
options: Waive the inspection, since a hospital serves the public
Arrange the inspection on priority and allow opening as soon as the ward passes
Refuse and take up the request in its normal turn
Ask the hospital to approach someone else
en.why: The inspection protects patients and cannot be waived. But the need is real, and what the officer can lawfully do is to speed up the inspection. The second option serves both.

en.stem: You are a new officer. You find that a register in your section has been filled in wrongly for months, apparently by oversight, before you joined. No loss is visible so far. What should you do?
options: Leave it, since it happened before your time
Correct the old entries yourself without telling anyone
Blame your predecessor in a note to all staff
Report the error to your senior with the facts, correct the practice from now, and have past entries set right in the proper way
en.why: The section is now your responsibility. Silent correction of old records is itself improper. The fourth option brings the error into the open and corrects it through the proper channel.

en.stem: You are an officer at a public counter. A man in the queue shouts that the staff are slow and others begin to join him. What should you do?
options: Go to the queue, hear the complaint calmly, tell people how long it will take, and open another counter if you can
Call the police to remove him
Close the counter until people calm down
Serve him first so that he goes away
en.why: The complaint may be fair, and information calms a queue. Serving the loudest person first is unfair to those waiting quietly. Police or closure is out of proportion.

en.stem: You are a block officer. A contractor's bill is ready for payment, but a field report says some of the work billed has not been done. The contractor says the report is wrong. What should you do?
options: Pay the bill in full to avoid a dispute
Blacklist the contractor at once
Have the work measured at the site in the contractor's presence and pay for what is found done
Keep the bill pending without giving a reason
en.why: The key fact is disputed and can be settled by measurement. Doing it in the contractor's presence makes the result fair to both sides.

en.stem: You are a hospital administrator. A nurse tells you privately that a senior doctor sometimes arrives for duty smelling of alcohol. What should you do?
options: Tell the nurse not to speak against seniors
Look into it without delay, discreetly, and if it is confirmed keep the doctor off patient duty and proceed under the rules, while protecting the nurse's identity
Announce the allegation to the staff
Wait to see whether a patient complains
en.why: Patient safety is at stake, so waiting is not acceptable. But the report is unverified, so the check must be quick and discreet, and the person who reported must be protected.

en.stem: You are a junior officer. At a meeting your senior presents figures that you know contain an error which changes the conclusion. What is the best course?
options: Stay silent; it is not your place
Tell other colleagues about the error after the meeting
Interrupt and say that the senior is wrong
Bring the error to the senior's notice at the first suitable moment, politely and with the correct figure, before a decision is taken on it
en.why: A decision on wrong figures harms the organisation, so silence fails. The fourth option corrects the error in time and with respect. Telling others afterwards helps no one.

en.stem: You are a forest officer. Villagers have for years collected fallen firewood from an area that has now been closed to entry by a new order. They ask you to let them continue. What should you do?
options: Explain the order, find out what the rules allow by way of other sources or permitted areas, and report the villagers' need to your seniors
Let them continue quietly
File cases against those who entered earlier
Tell them it is not your concern
en.why: The officer cannot set aside the order, and cannot ignore a real need. The first option keeps within the law, looks for a lawful alternative, and carries the problem to those who can change the rule.
